nameStory: Araneus iviei is named after scientist Dr. Michael Ivie, an entomologist who has made significant contributions to our understanding of North American insects and spiders. This species follows the scientific tradition of honoring researchers by incorporating their names into newly described species. The name celebrates Dr. Ivie's work in cataloging and identifying the diverse arthropod life of North America.
description: Araneus iviei is a member of the orbweaver family, known for spinning the classic circular webs we often picture when thinking of spider webs. Like other orbweavers, this species has a rounded abdomen and builds geometric webs to catch flying insects. This is a relatively uncommon spider in New England, with only a dozen confirmed sightings in the region. As with most orbweavers, females are typically larger than males, though specific size ranges for this species aren't well documented.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds the classic circular orb web with radiating spokes and spiral capture threads that feel sticky to the touch when accidentally walked into

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Rounded, bulbous abdomen typical of orbweavers, with the front part (cephalothorax) noticeably smaller and more compact

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in center of web waiting for prey, or hides nearby in a silk retreat connected to the web by a signal thread

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized orbweaver, with females noticeably larger than the smaller, more slender males

habitat: This uncommon orbweaver has been found in various habitats across New England, though specific habitat preferences aren't well documented due to limited observations. Like many orbweavers, it likely favors areas with suitable anchor points for web construction such as shrubs, trees, or tall vegetation. Given its rarity in our region, encountering one would be quite fortunate.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin appearing as temperatures warm, though peak activity likely occurs later in the season.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for web-building and feeding, when flying insect prey is abundant.
seasonality.fall: Mating season for most orbweavers, when males can be found searching for females in their webs.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures; species overwinters as eggs in protected silk sacs.

funFact: With only 12 recorded observations in all of New England, finding an Araneus iviei would make you part of a very exclusive club of naturalists who have encountered this elusive orbweaver in our region!
confusionNotes: Given the large number of orbweaver species in New England, Araneus iviei could easily be confused with its more common relatives like the Cross Orbweaver or Marbled Orbweaver. Definitive identification often requires expert examination of reproductive structures under magnification, making this a challenging species for casual observers to distinguish from other medium-sized orbweavers.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England means that most field guides and regional resources don't include detailed information about it. If you think you've found one, consider taking detailed photos and contacting local naturalist groups or university researchers who study spiders.
compareHints: Distinguishing Araneus iviei from its many orbweaver relatives in New England requires expert knowledge, as most species in this genus share similar web-building behavior and general body structure. Unlike the distinctive white cross pattern of the Cross Orbweaver or the marbled appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver, the specific markings and coloration that separate A. iviei from other species aren't well-documented in popular field guides. When in doubt with orbweavers, focus on overall patterns, web placement, and habitat rather than trying to identify rare species without expert help.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Marbled Orbweaver which has swirled, mottled patterns, the Cross Orbweaver's white cross marking is clean and distinct.

Among New England's Araneus orbweavers, the marbled orbweaver is unique for its extremely inflated, almost spherical abdomen—much rounder than the Cross Orbweaver's more egg-shaped belly or the Shamrock Orbweaver's triangular markings.

Among its Araneus cousins, the barn orbweaver is distinguished by its strong preference for wooden human structures, while the cross orbweaver favors gardens and the marbled orbweaver prefers trees and shrubs.

Among its Araneus cousins, the shamrock orbweaver's white spots make it relatively easy to distinguish - the cross orbweaver has a distinctive white cross pattern, while the marbled orbweaver shows complex marbled coloring without distinct dots.

Nordmann's Orbweaver is generally less distinctively marked than its famous cousins like the Cross Orbweaver (which has a prominent white cross pattern) or the Marbled Orbweaver (with its striking yellow and black marbled appearance).

Among the Araneus orbweavers, the Giant Lichen Orbweaver stands out for its specific lichen-mimicking camouflage, while relatives like the Cross Orbweaver have distinct white cross markings and the Marbled Orbweaver displays smooth, flowing color patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Fierce Orbweaver stands out for its bold behavioral responses rather than distinctive markings like the Cross Orbweaver's white cross or the Marbled Orbweaver's marbled patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Lattice Orbweaver's crosshatch pattern sets it apart from the distinctive white cross of the Cross Orbweaver and the swirled, marble-like patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Unlike the Cross Orbweaver which prefers gardens and woodland edges, or the Marbled Orbweaver found on trees, the Openfield Orbweaver specifically chooses exposed grasslands and meadows.

Among its Araneus relatives in New England, the Red-spotted Orbweaver is most easily distinguished by its reddish markings - the Cross Orbweaver has a white cross pattern, the Marbled Orbweaver has marbled yellow and brown coloring, and the Shamrock Orbweaver has a distinctive shamrock-like pattern.

Among the many Araneus orbweavers in New England, the Butterfly Orbweaver stands out for its wing-like geometric patterns rather than the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marble-stone appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Among its many Araneus relatives in New England, the Juniper Orbweaver's defining characteristic is its habitat specialization rather than distinctive markings.

Unlike the Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross pattern on the back, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its orange and white marbled appearance, the White-bellied Orbweaver's key feature is underneath rather than on top.

Among its Araneus cousins in New England, the Red-backed Orbweaver's bright green front section makes it stand out from the typically brown or gray Cross Orbweaver and the yellow-and-black patterned Marbled Orbweaver.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its mottled, marbled pattern, the Black-spotted Orbweaver displays clear black spots as its defining feature.

Unlike the abundant Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the variable Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, Araneus bonsallae lacks well-documented field marks for New England populations.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its white cross markings or the Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, the Humped bog orbweaver's most distinctive feature is its physical shape rather than its coloration.
